a: Producing a play begins with securing rights and paying royalties to the playwright or licensing agency (such as Samuel French, Dramatists Play Service, or Music Theatre International), which typically charges 8-12% of gross box office revenue for amateur productions or negotiated fees for professional runs. Creating a realistic budget covers theater rental or building costs, royalties, director and designer fees, actor salaries or stipends, costumes, sets, props, lighting, sound equipment, marketing, insurance, and contingency funds. Fundraising sources include ticket sales, grants from arts councils and foundations, individual donations via subscription campaigns, corporate sponsorships, and increasingly crowdfunding platforms like Kickstarter, with non-profit theaters often operating on a contributed-to-earned revenue ratio of roughly 60:40.

q: What does a theater director do?
How does a director cast a play?

a: The director is the primary artistic visionary responsible for interpreting the script, developing a directorial concept, casting actors, guiding rehearsals, and unifying all design elements into a cohesive production. Casting involves holding auditions (often including cold readings, prepared monologues, and callbacks) where the director assesses actors' suitability for each role based on type, chemistry with other actors, and ability to execute the required performance style. During rehearsals (typically 4-6 weeks for professional productions), the director sets blocking (staging the actors' movements on stage, traditionally notated in a prompt book), works on character development and scene dynamics, establishes pacing and rhythm, and conducts regular run-throughs leading to technical rehearsals where lighting, sound, set changes, and costumes are integrated. The director also collaborates closely with designers—set, costume, lighting, sound, and projection—in production meetings to ensure the visual and aural world supports the storytelling vision.

a: The stage manager is the organizational backbone of any theatrical production, responsible for scheduling rehearsals, creating and distributing rehearsal reports (daily documents detailing what was accomplished, what changed, and what needs attention), maintaining the prompt book with all blocking and cue notations, and calling all technical cues during performances. A cue sheet records every lighting change, sound effect, set movement, and fly-rail operation in sequence, indexed to specific lines or moments in the script, and is used by the stage manager to call cues over headset to the running crew during shows. Prop tracking involves creating a comprehensive prop list with descriptions, quantities, locations, and photos of every hand prop, set prop, and decorative item, then managing rehearsal props, acquiring or building final props, and running preshow checks to verify everything is in place before each performance.

a: The technical director (TD) manages the physical realization of the scenic design, overseeing construction, rigging, load-in, and strike of the set, while managing budgets, schedules, and safety protocols for scene shops and stage crews. Production meetings, convened weekly or more frequently as opening approaches, bring together the director, designers, stage manager, technical director, and producer to review progress, resolve conflicts, make budget decisions, and ensure all departments are synchronized toward the production's goals. Theater marketing involves creating a branding campaign (posters, postcards, social media content, email newsletters, press releases), securing media coverage, managing group sales, and implementing dynamic pricing strategies, while front of house operations manage the audience experience from ticketing at the box office through ushering, concessions, accessibility services, and post-show engagement.

a: Theater education programs encompass in-school residencies where teaching artists lead drama classes aligned with curriculum standards, after-school youth theater companies that produce full-scale productions with students, and adult education offerings like acting workshops and playwriting classes. Many theaters run audience enrichment programs such as pre-show lectures, post-show discussions with cast and creative teams, open rehearsals, and study guides that deepen understanding of the plays and their themes. Community engagement extends beyond education to include relaxed performances (for audiences with sensory sensitivities), sign-interpreted and audio-described performances for accessibility, partnerships with community organizations addressing relevant social issues, and devised theater projects created with specific community members to tell their own stories, all serving to democratize theater and build new, diverse audiences.
